lessons.title: Equivalence Relations and Partial Orders
lessons.content:
At the start of the year, a school sorts its students into houses: everyone born in the same month goes into the same group. Later, the timetable office plans the semester: Programming I must come before Programming II, and Discrete Maths must come before Algorithms. These two everyday tasks use the two most important kinds of relation. The first sorts things into groups of "the same kind": an equivalence relation. The second arranges things by "comes before": a partial order. Both appear constantly in computer science, from hashing and compilers to task scheduling and version control.

Equivalence relations: A relation on a set A is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. Elements related by an equivalence relation are called equivalent. Examples: "was born in the same month as" on people; "has the same length as" on strings; "a ≡ b (mod m)" on the integers; "lives in the same district as" on the population of Bangladesh. Each one says two things are "the same" in one particular respect, while possibly differing in others.

Congruence mod m is an equivalence relation: Reflexive: a − a = 0 is divisible by m. Symmetric: if m | (a − b) then m | (b − a), since b − a = −(a − b). Transitive: if m | (a − b) and m | (b − c), then m divides their sum, (a − b) + (b − c) = a − c. All three hold, so congruence mod m is an equivalence relation. This proof uses the divisibility facts from lesson 13.

Not equivalence relations: "is a friend of" is symmetric but usually not transitive. "≤" is reflexive and transitive but not symmetric. "differs by at most 1" on the integers is reflexive and symmetric but not transitive: 1 and 2 differ by 1, 2 and 3 differ by 1, but 1 and 3 differ by 2. Checking all three properties carefully is the whole job.

Equivalence classes: If R is an equivalence relation on A, the equivalence class of a is [a] = {s ∈ A | s R a}, all elements equivalent to a. Any element of a class is called a representative. For congruence mod 3 on the integers there are exactly three classes: [0] = {..., −3, 0, 3, 6, ...}, [1] = {..., −2, 1, 4, 7, ...} and [2] = {..., −1, 2, 5, 8, ...}. Note that [4] = [1], because 4 ≡ 1 (mod 3). These classes are the elements of Z₃ from lesson 13.

Classes form a partition: For an equivalence relation, the following are equivalent: a R b, [a] = [b], and [a] ∩ [b] ≠ ∅. So two classes are either identical or completely disjoint, and every element lies in its own class. Therefore the equivalence classes of R form a partition of A (lesson 8): non-empty, pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is A. Conversely, every partition of A defines an equivalence relation: "a and b are in the same part". Equivalence relations and partitions are two descriptions of the same thing.

Counting equivalence relations: Since equivalence relations correspond to partitions, counting one counts the other. A 3-element set {a, b, c} has 5 partitions: {a, b, c} as one block; {a, b}{c}; {a, c}{b}; {b, c}{a}; and {a}{b}{c}. So there are exactly 5 equivalence relations on a 3-element set, out of the 512 relations. These counts are called Bell numbers: 1, 2, 5, 15, 52 for sets of size 1 to 5.

Equivalence in computing: When a compiler decides whether two variable names refer to the same thing, when a spelling checker treats "Dhaka" and "dhaka" as equal, or when a hash table stores keys with the same hash value together, an equivalence relation is at work. The union-find data structure, which you will meet in Algorithms, maintains the classes of an equivalence relation as pairs are added, and is used in Kruskal's spanning tree algorithm from lesson 25.

Partial orders: A relation on a set S is a partial ordering if it is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive. The set with the relation, written (S, ≼), is a partially ordered set or poset. Examples: (Z, ≤); the positive integers with "divides"; the power set of a set with ⊆. Compared with an equivalence relation, the only change is symmetric replaced by antisymmetric, but the meaning changes completely: from "the same as" to "comes before or equal".

Comparable and incomparable: In a poset, a and b are comparable if a ≼ b or b ≼ a. Otherwise they are incomparable. Under "divides", 2 and 6 are comparable (2 | 6), but 2 and 3 are incomparable: neither divides the other. Under ⊆, {1} and {2} are incomparable. This is why it is called a partial order: not every pair has to be ordered. If every pair is comparable, the order is a total order (or linear order), like ≤ on the integers, and the set is called a chain.

Lexicographic order: Dictionaries order words letter by letter: compare the first letters; if they are equal, compare the second letters; and so on, with a shorter word that is a prefix coming first. So "cat" < "cattle" < "dog". Formally, on A × B with partial orders on A and B, (a₁, b₁) ≺ (a₂, b₂) if a₁ ≺ a₂, or a₁ = a₂ and b₁ ≺ b₂. Lexicographic order is how computers sort strings, file names and multi-column tables, such as sorting students by department and then by CGPA.

Hasse diagrams: A poset's digraph has many arrows, so we draw a simplified Hasse diagram. Start from the digraph, remove all loops (reflexivity is understood), remove every arrow implied by transitivity, and draw everything so arrows point upward, then remove the arrowheads. For the divisors of 12, {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12}, under "divides": 1 at the bottom, 2 and 3 above it, 4 above 2, 6 above both 2 and 3, and 12 at the top above 4 and 6. The edge from 1 to 4 is not drawn because it follows from 1 to 2 to 4.

Maximal, minimal, greatest, least: In a poset, a is maximal if no element is strictly above it, and minimal if no element is strictly below it. a is the greatest element if every element is ≼ a, and the least element if a ≼ every element. In the divisors of 12, 1 is least and 12 is greatest. In {2, 3, 4, 6} under "divides", the minimal elements are 2 and 3, the maximal ones are 4 and 6, and there is no least or greatest element. A poset can have many maximal elements but at most one greatest element.

Bounds and lattices: An upper bound of a subset is an element that is ≽ every element of the subset; the least upper bound (lub) is the smallest such bound, and the greatest lower bound (glb) is defined similarly. In the positive integers under "divides", lub(a, b) = lcm(a, b) and glb(a, b) = gcd(a, b): for 4 and 6, the lub is 12 and the glb is 2. A poset in which every pair has both a lub and a glb is called a lattice. The power set with ⊆ is a lattice, with lub = union and glb = intersection. Lattices are used in program analysis and in security models of information flow.

Topological sorting: Every finite non-empty poset has at least one minimal element. Using this, we can list the elements in a total order that respects the partial order, called a topological sort: repeatedly pick a minimal element, write it down and remove it. A topological sort is exactly what you need to schedule tasks with prerequisites. Most posets have several valid topological sorts.

Topological sort example: A software project has tasks: design (D), database (B), backend (K), frontend (F), testing (T), release (R). Prerequisites: D before B, D before F, B before K, K before T, F before T, T before R. Minimal: D. Remove it; now B and F are minimal, pick B. Then K and F are minimal, pick K. Then F. Then T. Then R. One valid order: D, B, K, F, T, R. Another: D, F, B, K, T, R. Build tools like make, package managers like npm and pip, and spreadsheet recalculation all perform topological sorts.

Well-ordered sets: A poset is well-ordered if it is a total order and every non-empty subset has a least element. The natural numbers with ≤ are well-ordered, which is the well-ordering property from lesson 11. The integers with ≤ are not, because the set of negative integers has no least element. Well-ordered sets support induction, and computer scientists use them to prove that loops and recursive programs terminate: if each step moves to a strictly smaller element of a well-ordered set, the process cannot go on forever.

Real-life example 1, sorting by blood group at a hospital: A hospital in Rajshahi groups patients by blood group: "has the same blood group as" is an equivalence relation, and its classes A+, A−, B+, B−, AB+, AB−, O+, O− partition the patient list. When an emergency needs O− blood, the system looks at just that class. Meanwhile, "can safely donate red cells to" behaves like an order: O− donors can give to everyone, AB+ patients can receive from everyone. Two different relation types, both essential in a blood bank database.

Real-life example 2, the CSE course plan: A university's CSE curriculum lists prerequisites: Structured Programming before Data Structures, Data Structures before Algorithms, Discrete Mathematics before Algorithms and Theory of Computation, Digital Logic before Computer Architecture, and so on. "Must be taken before or is the same as" is a partial order on courses; many pairs, like Digital Logic and Discrete Mathematics, are incomparable and can be taken in either order. The academic office builds each student's semester plan with a topological sort, and a Hasse diagram of the courses is often printed in the student handbook.

Common mistakes: Calling a relation an equivalence relation after checking only two properties. Confusing equivalence classes with the elements themselves. Forgetting that a partial order need not compare every pair. Drawing Hasse diagrams with transitive edges or with loops. Mixing up maximal and greatest: a maximal element just has nothing above it, while the greatest is above everything. And assuming a topological sort is unique.

What exams ask: Prove a relation is an equivalence relation (often congruence or "same something"); find equivalence classes and the corresponding partition; count equivalence relations or partitions on a small set; check whether a relation is a partial order; draw Hasse diagrams for divisor sets or power sets; find maximal, minimal, greatest and least elements, bounds, lub and glb; decide whether a poset is a lattice; and produce a topological sort for a set of tasks.

Recap: An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive; its classes partition the set, and partitions give equivalence relations back. A partial order is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive; some pairs may be incomparable. Hasse diagrams draw posets cleanly. Maximal, minimal, greatest and least elements, bounds and lattices describe their structure, and topological sorting turns a partial order into a schedule. Next lesson we start the final big area of the course: graphs.

lessons.title: Graphs: Basics, Types and Representations
lessons.content:
Draw a dot for each of your friends and a line between two dots when those two people know each other. Draw a dot for every bus stop in Dhaka and a line for every road between neighbouring stops. Draw a dot for every web page and an arrow for every link. In each case you have made a graph: a set of dots joined by lines. Graphs are one of the most useful ideas in all of computer science, because almost anything with connections can be modelled as one. This lesson covers the vocabulary, the main types of graphs, the handshaking theorem, how computers store graphs, and how to tell when two graphs are really the same.

What a graph is: A graph G = (V, E) consists of a non-empty set V of vertices (also called nodes) and a set E of edges, where each edge connects two vertices, called its endpoints. If V = {A, B, C, D} and E = {AB, BC, CD, DA}, the graph is a square. The picture is just a convenience: what matters is which pairs are connected, not where the dots are drawn or whether the lines are straight.

Types of graphs: A simple graph has undirected edges, no loops (edges from a vertex to itself) and at most one edge between any pair of vertices; a friendship network is simple. A multigraph allows several edges between the same pair, like several roads joining two towns. A pseudograph also allows loops. A directed graph (digraph) has directed edges, arrows from one vertex to another, like "follows" on Instagram or one-way streets in Old Dhaka. Choosing the right type is the first modelling decision.

Basic terminology: Two vertices are adjacent (neighbours) if an edge joins them, and that edge is incident with both. The degree of a vertex, deg(v), is the number of edges incident with it, where a loop counts twice. A vertex of degree 0 is isolated; a vertex of degree 1 is pendant. The neighbourhood N(v) is the set of neighbours of v. In a friendship graph, deg(v) is how many friends v has.

The handshaking theorem: In any undirected graph with m edges, the sum of all degrees equals 2m. Why? Each edge has two ends and contributes exactly 2 to the degree sum, one at each end. Example: a graph with 10 vertices, each of degree 6, has degree sum 60, so it has 60/2 = 30 edges. The name comes from a party: if everyone counts how many hands they shook, the total is twice the number of handshakes.

A consequence: An undirected graph always has an even number of vertices of odd degree. The degree sum 2m is even; the even degrees add to an even number, so the odd degrees must also add to an even number, which requires an even count of them. So it is impossible for a party of 7 people to have everyone shake hands with exactly 3 others: that would give 7 odd degrees. This is the same argument as the cricket league in lesson 6.

Directed graphs and degrees: In a digraph, an edge (u, v) goes from u, its initial vertex, to v, its terminal vertex. The in-degree deg⁻(v) is the number of edges coming into v, and the out-degree deg⁺(v) is the number leaving v. The sum of all in-degrees equals the sum of all out-degrees equals the number of edges, since each arrow has one tail and one head. On Twitter-like apps, in-degree is your follower count and out-degree is how many you follow.

Complete graphs: The complete graph Kₙ has n vertices and an edge between every pair. It has C(n, 2) = n(n − 1)/2 edges: K₃ is a triangle with 3 edges, K₄ has 6, K₅ has 10. A round-robin tournament where every team plays every other team once is Kₙ: 10 teams play 45 matches. Every vertex in Kₙ has degree n − 1.

Cycles, wheels and cubes: The cycle Cₙ (n ≥ 3) is n vertices in a ring, with n edges, each vertex of degree 2. The wheel Wₙ adds a hub vertex joined to every vertex of Cₙ, giving n + 1 vertices and 2n edges. The n-cube Qₙ has a vertex for each of the 2ⁿ bit strings of length n, with an edge when two strings differ in exactly one bit. Q₃ is the corners and edges of an ordinary cube. Qₙ has n·2ⁿ⁻¹ edges, and it was used as the connection pattern in some parallel computers.

Bipartite graphs: A simple graph is bipartite if its vertices can be split into two sets V₁ and V₂ such that every edge goes between V₁ and V₂, never inside one set. Example: students and the courses they take, with edges only from a student to a course. A graph is bipartite exactly when you can colour its vertices with two colours so that no edge joins two vertices of the same colour, and that happens exactly when the graph has no cycle of odd length. C₆ is bipartite (alternate colours around the ring); C₅ and K₃ are not.

Complete bipartite graphs and matchings: The complete bipartite graph Kₘ,ₙ has parts of sizes m and n with every possible edge between them, so mn edges. K₃,₃ appears in the famous "three houses and three utilities" puzzle of lesson 24. Bipartite graphs model assignment problems: matching job applicants to jobs, students to project supervisors, or riders to passengers in a ride-sharing app. A matching is a set of edges with no shared vertex; finding the largest matching is a classic algorithmic problem.

New graphs from old: A subgraph of G uses some of G's vertices and some of the edges between them. Removing a vertex removes its incident edges too. The union of two graphs takes all vertices and all edges of both. The complement of a simple graph G has the same vertices, with an edge exactly where G has none: the complement of K₄ minus one edge is a single edge plus two isolated vertices. A graph with every vertex of the same degree k is called k-regular, such as Cₙ (2-regular) and Kₙ ((n − 1)-regular).

Adjacency lists: Computers need to store graphs. An adjacency list records, for each vertex, the list of its neighbours. For the square A–B–C–D–A: A: B, D; B: A, C; C: B, D; D: C, A. The total length of all lists is 2m for an undirected graph (each edge appears twice) and m for a directed one. Adjacency lists use memory proportional to n + m, which is ideal for sparse graphs like road networks and social networks where most pairs are not connected.

Adjacency matrices: An adjacency matrix is an n × n matrix with a 1 in row i, column j if vertices i and j are adjacent, and 0 otherwise. For an undirected simple graph it is symmetric with zeros on the diagonal, and the sum of row i is deg(i). It uses n² entries no matter how many edges there are, which is wasteful for sparse graphs (a city with 10,000 junctions needs 100 million entries), but it answers "are i and j adjacent?" instantly. Multigraphs store the number of edges in each entry. An incidence matrix, with rows for vertices and columns for edges, is a third option used less often.

Graph isomorphism: Two graphs G₁ and G₂ are isomorphic if there is a bijection f from V₁ to V₂ such that u and v are adjacent in G₁ exactly when f(u) and f(v) are adjacent in G₂. Isomorphic graphs are the same graph drawn differently or with different names. A square drawn as a diamond, or with vertices labelled 1, 2, 3, 4, is still C₄. To show isomorphism, give the bijection and check every edge.

Showing graphs are not isomorphic: Isomorphic graphs share every structural property, called an invariant: the number of vertices, the number of edges, the degree sequence (the list of degrees sorted), being bipartite, having a cycle of a given length, and so on. If any invariant differs, the graphs are not isomorphic. Example: C₆ and two separate triangles both have 6 vertices, 6 edges and every degree 2, but C₆ has no triangle while the other has two, so they are not isomorphic. Matching invariants do not prove isomorphism; for that you still need a bijection. No fast algorithm is known that decides isomorphism for every pair of graphs, though very good practical methods exist.

Real-life example 1, Facebook as a graph: Facebook's friendship network is a huge simple undirected graph with billions of vertices. Your degree is your number of friends. "People you may know" suggestions look at vertices two steps away that share many neighbours with you. The network is sparse, since each person has at most thousands of friends among billions of users, so it is stored with adjacency lists, not a matrix. Instagram and X (Twitter) use directed graphs because following is one-way. Many social network analysis ideas, like finding influential people, are degree and path calculations on these graphs.

Real-life example 2, Dhaka's metro and roads: Model each station of the MRT Line-6 as a vertex and each track segment between consecutive stations as an edge. The line from Uttara North to Motijheel forms a path graph, where the end stations have degree 1 and the others degree 2. When future lines cross, interchange stations will have degree 3 or 4. Adding Old Dhaka's one-way streets turns part of the road graph into a digraph, and adding travel times as edge weights prepares it for the shortest-path algorithms of the next lesson.

Common mistakes: Counting a loop as adding 1 to the degree instead of 2. Forgetting the handshaking theorem means the number of edges is half the degree sum. Assuming every graph with matching vertex and edge counts is isomorphic. Calling a graph bipartite without checking for odd cycles. Mixing up in-degree and out-degree. And using an adjacency matrix for a huge sparse graph in code, which can run out of memory.

What exams ask: Identify the type of a graph; find degrees and verify the handshaking theorem; use it to show some degree sequences are impossible; count edges of Kₙ, Cₙ, Wₙ, Qₙ and Kₘ,ₙ; decide whether a graph is bipartite and give the two parts; write adjacency lists and matrices and draw a graph from a matrix; and decide whether two graphs are isomorphic, giving a bijection or a differing invariant.

Recap: A graph is vertices plus edges; it may be simple, multi, pseudo or directed. The handshaking theorem says Σ deg(v) = 2m, so odd-degree vertices come in even numbers. Kₙ has n(n − 1)/2 edges, Kₘ,ₙ has mn, and bipartite graphs are exactly those without odd cycles. Graphs are stored as adjacency lists or matrices, and isomorphism means the same structure under relabelling. Next lesson we travel along graphs: paths, connectivity, Euler and Hamilton paths, shortest paths, planarity and colouring.

lessons.title: Graph Paths, Euler and Hamilton, Shortest Paths, Planarity, Colouring
lessons.content:
In the 1700s, the town of Königsberg had seven bridges joining two islands and the two river banks. People wondered: can you take a walk that crosses every bridge exactly once? Nobody could find one, but nobody could prove it impossible either, until the mathematician Leonhard Euler solved it in 1736 by turning the town into dots and lines. That was the birth of graph theory. In this lesson we travel along graphs: paths and connectivity, Euler's bridges, Hamilton's tours, shortest routes like the ones Google Maps finds, graphs that can be drawn without crossings, and colouring problems like exam timetables.

Paths and circuits: A path of length n in a graph is a sequence of n edges where each edge starts where the previous one ended, like v₀ → v₁ → ... → vₙ. A circuit (or cycle) is a path that starts and ends at the same vertex. A path is simple if it does not repeat an edge. In some books "path" allows repeated vertices and edges, and the word "walk" is used for that; always check your textbook's definitions, because exam answers depend on them.

Connectivity: An undirected graph is connected if there is a path between every pair of vertices. A graph that is not connected splits into connected components, maximal connected pieces. A road network with an island not reachable by road has at least two components. A cut vertex is a vertex whose removal increases the number of components, and a cut edge, or bridge, is an edge whose removal does the same. In a computer network, cut vertices and bridges are single points of failure that engineers try to eliminate with backup links.

Connectivity in directed graphs: A directed graph is strongly connected if there is a directed path from every vertex to every other vertex, following the arrows. It is weakly connected if it is connected when you ignore the directions. A one-way street system in a city must be strongly connected, or some places would be impossible to reach by car. Web pages are far from strongly connected: you can often follow links into a page but not back out.

Counting walks with matrices: If A is the adjacency matrix of a graph, then the entry in row i, column j of Aʳ counts the number of walks of length r from vertex i to vertex j. For a triangle, A² has 2 on the diagonal (two ways to go out and come back) and 1 elsewhere. This connects graphs to the matrix multiplication you meet in linear algebra, and it is the basis of some ranking algorithms, including ideas behind Google's original PageRank.

Euler circuits and paths: An Euler circuit is a circuit that uses every edge exactly once; an Euler path uses every edge exactly once but may end somewhere else. Euler's theorem: a connected multigraph with at least two vertices has an Euler circuit if and only if every vertex has even degree. It has an Euler path that is not a circuit if and only if it has exactly two vertices of odd degree, and the path must start at one of them and end at the other. The reason: every time you pass through a vertex you use two of its edges, one in and one out.

Solving Königsberg: Make each land area a vertex and each bridge an edge. The four vertices have degrees 5, 3, 3 and 3. All four are odd. An Euler circuit needs zero odd vertices and an Euler path needs exactly two, so neither exists: the walk is impossible. Euler did not need to try every route; one look at the degrees settled it. This is the power of finding the right invariant.

Euler paths in practice: The same check answers whether a drawing can be traced without lifting your pen and without retracing a line, a common children's puzzle. It also helps route planning when every street must be covered: a city corporation garbage truck, a postman, or a snow plough. If some vertices have odd degree, the best route must repeat some streets, and finding which ones to repeat is called the Chinese postman problem, which can be solved efficiently.

Hamilton paths and circuits: A Hamilton path visits every vertex exactly once; a Hamilton circuit also returns to the start. This sounds similar to Euler's problem, with vertices instead of edges, but it is far harder. No simple test like "check the degrees" is known, and deciding whether a Hamilton circuit exists is NP-complete, meaning no fast algorithm is known for all graphs. Some sufficient conditions exist: Dirac's theorem says that if a simple graph has n ≥ 3 vertices and every vertex has degree at least n/2, it has a Hamilton circuit. Ore's theorem gives a similar condition using pairs of non-adjacent vertices.

Hamilton examples: Every complete graph Kₙ with n ≥ 3 has a Hamilton circuit: visit the vertices in any order. The cube Q₃ has one, corresponding to the Gray code 000, 001, 011, 010, 110, 111, 101, 100, where consecutive codes differ in one bit, used in rotary encoders and error reduction. A graph with a vertex of degree 1 cannot have a Hamilton circuit, because a circuit needs two edges at every vertex. A star graph cannot even have a Hamilton path when it has more than two leaves.

Weighted graphs and the travelling salesperson problem: Often edges carry numbers, called weights: distances, travel times or costs. The travelling salesperson problem (TSP) asks for a Hamilton circuit of minimum total weight: a salesperson must visit every city once and return home as cheaply as possible. With n cities there are (n − 1)!/2 different circuits to compare, which explodes quickly, as lesson 17 showed. Delivery companies and chip designers use approximation algorithms that find routes close to optimal in reasonable time.

Shortest paths: A much easier problem is the shortest path between two vertices in a weighted graph. Dijkstra's algorithm solves it when all weights are non-negative. Idea: keep a tentative distance for each vertex, starting with 0 for the source and infinity for the rest. Repeatedly pick the unvisited vertex with the smallest tentative distance, mark it as final, and update its neighbours: if going through it gives a shorter route, lower their tentative distance. When the target is marked final, its distance is the answer.

Dijkstra worked example: Vertices A, B, C, D, E with edges A–B 4, A–C 2, C–B 1, B–D 5, C–D 8, C–E 10, D–E 2. Start at A with distance 0. Neighbours: B = 4, C = 2. Pick C (2): update B to min(4, 2 + 1) = 3, D to 2 + 8 = 10, E to 2 + 10 = 12. Pick B (3): update D to min(10, 3 + 5) = 8. Pick D (8): update E to min(12, 8 + 2) = 10. Pick E (10). The shortest route from A to E has length 10, along A, C, B, D, E. Notice the direct-looking route A, C, E costs 12; the algorithm finds the cheaper detour.

Planar graphs: A graph is planar if it can be drawn in the plane with no edges crossing. K₄ is planar: draw a triangle and put the fourth vertex in the middle. The question matters for designing circuit boards, where crossing wires need extra layers, and for drawing maps. The famous puzzle: can three houses each be connected to three utilities (water, gas, electricity) without any lines crossing? That graph is K₃,₃, and the answer is no.

Euler's formula: For a connected planar simple graph drawn without crossings, with v vertices, e edges and r regions (including the outer unbounded region), v − e + r = 2. Check with a cube drawn flat: 8 vertices, 12 edges, 6 regions: 8 − 12 + 6 = 2. A consequence: if v ≥ 3, then e ≤ 3v − 6, because every region is bounded by at least 3 edges. K₅ has v = 5 and e = 10, but 3v − 6 = 9, so K₅ is not planar. For graphs with no triangles, every region needs at least 4 edges, giving e ≤ 2v − 4; K₃,₃ has e = 9 > 2 × 6 − 4 = 8, so it is not planar. Kuratowski's theorem says, roughly, that K₅ and K₃,₃ are the only two fundamental obstacles to planarity.

Graph colouring: A colouring of a graph assigns a colour to each vertex so that adjacent vertices get different colours. The chromatic number χ(G) is the fewest colours needed. χ(Kₙ) = n, since every pair is adjacent. χ(Cₙ) is 2 for even n and 3 for odd n. A graph with at least one edge has χ = 2 exactly when it is bipartite. The four colour theorem states that every planar graph can be coloured with at most 4 colours, so any map can be coloured with 4 colours so that neighbouring regions differ. It was proved in 1976 by Appel and Haken with heavy use of a computer, one of the first major computer-assisted proofs.

Colouring in practice: Colouring models conflicts. In exam scheduling, each course is a vertex and an edge joins two courses that share a student; colours are time slots, and χ(G) is the minimum number of slots with no clashes. Compilers colour an "interference graph" of variables to assign them to a limited number of CPU registers. Mobile network operators colour cells so that neighbouring towers use different frequencies. Finding χ(G) exactly is hard in general, so practical systems use good greedy heuristics.

Real-life example 1, Google Maps through Dhaka traffic: When you ask for a route from Mohammadpur to Banani, the map service treats junctions as vertices and road segments as weighted edges, where the weight is the expected travel time given current traffic. Shortest-path algorithms based on Dijkstra's idea, with extra speed-ups for huge maps, find the fastest route. When a road is closed for a rally, that edge is removed, and if it was a bridge in the graph sense, part of the city can only be reached by a long detour. One-way streets make the graph directed, and the route must follow the arrows.

Real-life example 2, scheduling term finals at a college: A college in Barishal has 7 courses and must schedule final exams so that no student has two exams at once. The exam office draws a conflict graph: an edge between two courses whenever some student takes both. If the graph contains a triangle, at least 3 slots are needed. Using a greedy colouring, assigning each course the first slot not used by its neighbours, they find a timetable with 3 slots, matching the lower bound, so 3 is optimal. Graph colouring has just saved two exam days.

Common mistakes: Confusing Euler (every edge once) with Hamilton (every vertex once). Forgetting that an Euler path must start and end at the two odd-degree vertices. Assuming a graph without an obvious Hamilton circuit has none, or applying Dirac's condition in reverse: failing it does not prove there is no circuit. Using Dijkstra with negative weights. Forgetting the outer region in Euler's formula. And thinking that e ≤ 3v − 6 proves planarity; it can only prove non-planarity.

What exams ask: Decide whether graphs are connected, find components, cut vertices and bridges; decide whether Euler circuits or paths exist and find one; explain the Königsberg problem; find Hamilton paths or argue none exist, and apply Dirac's theorem; run Dijkstra's algorithm on a small weighted graph, showing the table; use Euler's formula and its corollaries to show K₅ and K₃,₃ are not planar; and find chromatic numbers and solve a scheduling problem by colouring.

Recap: Paths and circuits move along edges; connected graphs have paths between all pairs, and cut vertices and bridges are weak points. Euler circuits need all even degrees, Euler paths exactly two odd ones. Hamilton circuits are much harder, with only sufficient conditions like Dirac's. Dijkstra finds shortest paths with non-negative weights. Planar graphs satisfy v − e + r = 2, which rules out K₅ and K₃,₃. Colouring models conflicts, and every planar graph needs at most 4 colours. Next lesson ends the course with the most important special graphs: trees.

Euler circuit ⇔ connected with all degrees even; Euler path ⇔ exactly two odd vertices.
Königsberg (degrees 5, 3, 3, 3) has no Euler path: graph theory's first theorem.
Hamilton circuits visit every vertex once; no easy test (NP-complete); Dirac: all degrees ≥ n/2 is sufficient.
Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths when weights are non-negative.
Planar graphs: v − e + r = 2 and e ≤ 3v − 6; K₅ and K₃,₃ are not planar.
Chromatic number χ(G): χ(Kₙ) = n, χ(even cycle) = 2, χ(odd cycle) = 3; four colour theorem for planar graphs.
lessons.tip: Euler is about Edges, Hamilton is about vertices: remember "E for Euler, E for Edges".

lessons.title: Trees and Spanning Trees
lessons.content:
Open the file manager on your computer: a C drive, inside it folders, inside those more folders and files. Look at a family tree on the wall of your grandparents' house: one ancestor at the top, branching down through generations. Think of a knockout cricket tournament: matches pair up, winners move up, until one champion remains. All three are trees, graphs with branches but no loops. Trees are the single most used structure in computer science: they organise file systems, databases, compilers, search engines, compression, networks and AI decision making. This final lesson brings together graphs, recursion, induction and counting to study them.

What a tree is: A tree is a connected undirected graph with no simple circuits. A graph with no simple circuits that is not necessarily connected is a forest; each of its connected components is a tree. Trees are the "minimal" connected graphs: remove any edge and the graph falls apart; add any edge and a circuit appears. A path graph, a star, and the line of stations on a metro line are all trees.

Key properties: An undirected graph is a tree exactly when there is a unique simple path between any two of its vertices. A tree with n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges. Proof idea by induction: a tree with at least 2 vertices has a leaf (a vertex of degree 1); removing it and its edge leaves a tree with n − 1 vertices and, by the inductive hypothesis, n − 2 edges, so the original had n − 1. Conversely, a connected graph with n vertices and n − 1 edges is a tree. A forest with n vertices and c components has n − c edges.

Rooted trees: Choosing one vertex as the root and directing every edge away from it gives a rooted tree. Words come from family trees: if u → v is an edge, u is the parent of v and v is a child of u. Vertices with the same parent are siblings. Ancestors are vertices on the path up to the root; descendants are those below. A vertex with no children is a leaf, and one with children is internal. A subtree is a vertex together with all its descendants. The level of a vertex is the length of the path from the root to it, and the height of the tree is the largest level.

m-ary trees: A rooted tree is m-ary if every internal vertex has at most m children, and full m-ary if every internal vertex has exactly m children. With m = 2 we get binary trees, where each child is called the left or right child. Counting facts for a full m-ary tree with i internal vertices: it has n = mi + 1 vertices (every vertex except the root is a child of exactly one internal vertex) and l = (m − 1)i + 1 leaves. A full binary tree with 7 internal vertices has 15 vertices and 8 leaves.

Height and balance: An m-ary tree of height h has at most mʰ leaves. Turning this around, a tree with l leaves has height at least ⌈log_m l⌉. A rooted tree is balanced if all leaves are at level h or h − 1. Balanced binary trees with n vertices have height about log₂ n, which is the secret behind fast searching: a balanced tree holding a million items has height about 20.

Knockout tournaments: A knockout tournament with 16 teams is a full binary tree with 16 leaves (the teams) and 15 internal vertices (the matches). Since l = i + 1 for full binary trees, a knockout with t teams always has exactly t − 1 matches: every match eliminates one team, and all but the champion must be eliminated. The height, log₂ 16 = 4, is the number of rounds.

Binary search trees: A binary search tree (BST) stores keys so that, for every vertex, all keys in its left subtree are smaller and all keys in its right subtree are larger. To insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80 in that order: 50 is the root; 30 goes left; 70 goes right; 20 goes left of 30; 40 goes right of 30; 60 goes left of 70; 80 goes right of 70. The result is perfectly balanced with height 2. Searching for 60 compares with 50 (go right), 70 (go left), 60 (found): three comparisons. Search time grows with the height, so balanced BSTs give fast lookups, while inserting keys in sorted order produces a long thin tree as slow as a list.

Decision trees: A decision tree models an algorithm that makes comparisons: each internal vertex is a question, each branch an answer, and each leaf an outcome. Example: among 8 coins, one fake coin is lighter. A balance scale has three outcomes (left heavier, right heavier, balanced), so the decision tree is 3-ary with at least 8 leaves, needing height at least ⌈log₃ 8⌉ = 2. Two weighings suffice: weigh 3 against 3; if they balance, weigh the remaining 2 against each other; otherwise weigh 2 of the 3 lighter-side coins against each other.

The sorting lower bound: Any sorting algorithm based on comparing pairs of items is a binary decision tree whose leaves are all n! possible orders of the input. A binary tree with n! leaves has height at least ⌈log₂ n!⌉, which grows like n log₂ n. So no comparison sort can beat about n log₂ n comparisons in the worst case, and merge sort from lesson 12 is optimal in this sense. For 3 items, n! = 6, so at least ⌈log₂ 6⌉ = 3 comparisons are needed in the worst case.

Prefix codes: To store text in fewer bits, we can give frequent letters shorter codes. To decode without separators, no code may be the beginning (prefix) of another: such a code is a prefix code. Prefix codes correspond to binary trees: each letter sits at a leaf, and its code is the path from the root, with 0 for left and 1 for right. For example A = 0, B = 10, C = 110, D = 111 is a prefix code, and 0101100 decodes uniquely as A, B, C, A.

Huffman coding: Huffman's algorithm builds an optimal prefix code from letter frequencies. Start with each letter as a one-vertex tree weighted by its frequency. Repeatedly join the two trees of smallest weight under a new root whose weight is their sum, until one tree remains. Example: frequencies A 5, B 2, C 1, D 1. Join C and D (weight 2). Join that with B (weight 4). Join with A (weight 9). Codes: A = 0, B = 10, C = 110, D = 111. Total bits for the 9 letters: 5 × 1 + 2 × 2 + 1 × 3 + 1 × 3 = 15, versus 18 with a fixed 2 bits per letter. Huffman coding is part of formats like ZIP (DEFLATE), JPEG and MP3.

Tree traversals: Many programs must visit every vertex of a rooted tree. Preorder visits the root, then each subtree in preorder. Inorder (for binary trees) visits the left subtree, the root, then the right subtree. Postorder visits each subtree in postorder, then the root. An inorder traversal of a BST lists the keys in sorted order: for the BST above, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80. A file manager computing folder sizes uses postorder, since a folder's size needs its children's sizes first.

Expression trees: The expression (3 + 4) × 5 can be stored as a binary tree with × at the root, the subtree for 3 + 4 on the left and 5 on the right. Preorder gives × + 3 4 5 (Polish or prefix notation). Inorder gives 3 + 4 × 5, which needs brackets to be read correctly. Postorder gives 3 4 + 5 × (reverse Polish or postfix notation), which a computer can evaluate with a simple stack and no brackets: push 3, push 4, + gives 7, push 5, × gives 35. Compilers and calculators use exactly this.

Spanning trees: A spanning tree of a connected graph G is a subgraph that is a tree and includes every vertex of G. Every connected graph has one: keep removing edges from circuits until no circuit remains. Depth-first search (DFS), which goes as deep as possible before backtracking, and breadth-first search (BFS), which explores level by level, both produce spanning trees, and are the two basic graph exploration algorithms you will implement in Data Structures. The complete graph Kₙ has nⁿ⁻² different spanning trees (Cayley's formula); K₄ has 16.

Minimum spanning trees: In a weighted connected graph, a minimum spanning tree (MST) is a spanning tree with the smallest total weight. Kruskal's algorithm: sort edges by weight and keep adding the cheapest edge that does not form a circuit, until n − 1 edges are chosen. Prim's algorithm: start from any vertex and repeatedly add the cheapest edge joining the tree to a new vertex. Both are greedy algorithms that provably give an optimal tree. Example with vertices A, B, C, D and edges AB 1, BC 2, AD 3, AC 4, BD 5, CD 6: Kruskal picks AB (1), BC (2), skips nothing yet, picks AD (3); now 3 edges for 4 vertices, total weight 6. Prim from A picks AB (1), then BC (2), then AD (3): the same tree.

Real-life example 1, connecting upazilas with fibre: A telecom company wants to connect 8 upazilas in a district with fibre-optic cable so that every upazila can reach every other, using the least cable. The possible cable routes and their lengths form a weighted graph, and the cheapest connected network that reaches everyone is a minimum spanning tree, because any extra cable would create a loop that is not needed. Kruskal's or Prim's algorithm finds it. Electricity grids, water pipelines and computer network designers solve the same problem, sometimes adding a few extra links on purpose for backup, accepting a higher cost for reliability.

Real-life example 2, how your phone finds a contact: When you type a name into your phone's contacts search, the phone does not scan every contact one by one. Contacts are stored in a balanced search-tree-like structure ordered by name (many systems use B-trees or similar trees, which are m-ary search trees designed for storage). With 2,000 contacts, a balanced binary search would need about 11 comparisons, since 2¹¹ = 2048. Databases at banks and national ID servers rely on the same idea to find one record among crores in a fraction of a second.

Common mistakes: Forgetting that a tree must be connected, or confusing "no circuits" with "no cycles of length 3". Miscounting edges: always n − 1 for a tree. Mixing up height (longest root-to-leaf path) and number of levels (height + 1). In BSTs, putting equal or larger keys on the left. In Huffman coding, joining the two largest instead of the two smallest weights. In Kruskal's algorithm, adding an edge that creates a circuit. And confusing preorder and postorder in expression trees.

What exams ask: Prove that a tree with n vertices has n − 1 edges; use the formulas n = mi + 1 and l = (m − 1)i + 1; find height, levels, parents, ancestors and leaves in a rooted tree; build a BST from a list and search it; draw decision trees for coin-weighing puzzles; give the comparison-sort lower bound; build Huffman codes and compute average code length; perform preorder, inorder and postorder traversals and convert expressions between prefix, infix and postfix; and find minimum spanning trees with Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms.

Course recap: Trees are connected graphs without circuits, with n − 1 edges and unique paths. Rooted, m-ary and binary trees organise data; BSTs and balanced trees make searching fast; decision trees prove lower bounds; Huffman trees compress data; traversals visit every vertex; and minimum spanning trees connect everything cheaply. Looking back over the whole course, you have learned to state things precisely (logic), prove them (proof methods and induction), describe collections and connections (sets, functions, relations), compute with whole numbers (number theory), count and estimate chances (combinatorics and probability), analyse recursive processes (recurrences), and model networks (graphs and trees). These are the foundations every later CSE course builds on. Well done for reaching the end.
key_points: A tree is a connected graph with no simple circuits; it has n − 1 edges and unique paths between vertices.
Rooted trees: parent, child, sibling, ancestor, leaf, internal vertex, level, height.
Full m-ary tree with i internal vertices: n = mi + 1 vertices, l = (m − 1)i + 1 leaves; height ≥ ⌈log_m l⌉.
Binary search trees give search time proportional to height; balanced trees have height about log₂ n.
Decision trees give lower bounds, e.g. comparison sorting needs about n log₂ n comparisons.
Huffman coding builds optimal prefix codes by merging the two smallest weights.
Traversals: preorder, inorder (sorted for BSTs), postorder (reverse Polish); MSTs via Kruskal and Prim.
